entries.clue: Directions announced for seamstress and farmer somewhere in London (4)

indicatorNotes.announced: what is announced is heard, so the letters come from the sound of the words

blocks.note: the directions are spoken orders, one word each, to the two workers that follow
the instruction you give a seamstress is 'Sew!'
the instruction you give a farmer is 'Hoe!'

annotation.surface: Someone shouts out orders to a seamstress and a farmer, somewhere in the capital.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Directions' is not compass points here but commands: 'Sew!' for the seamstress, 'Hoe!' for the farmer. Soho is a district of central London.
annotation.definitionFit: Soho is a district in London's West End, so it is somewhere in London.

entries.clue: Dresses cut outrageously – for this one? (10)

annotation.definition: Dresses cut outrageously – for this one?

indicatorNotes.outrageously: outrageously means wildly, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A question about who wears dresses cut in a daring, revealing way.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: a seductress is the sort who wears outrageously cut dresses. The dash and question mark flag the double reading.
annotation.definitionFit: A seductress is the woman for whom a daringly cut dress would be chosen.

entries.clue: Duke included in inquiry about health? The nerve! (3,4,3)

indicatorNotes.included in: what is included in something sits inside it, so D goes inside HOW ARE YOU

blocks.note: first part of 'How are you?', the everyday question about someone's health
D is the abbreviation for duke
the rest of 'How are you?'

annotation.surface: A duke is asked how he is feeling and takes offence at the cheek of it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About health' belongs to the inquiry, not to a reversal or container; it simply tells you the question is 'How are you?'.
annotation.definitionFit: 'How dare you!' and 'The nerve!' are both indignant exclamations at someone's cheek.

entries.clue: This may show you a rainbow meandering for certain (10)

annotation.definition: This may show you a rainbow

indicatorNotes.meandering: something meandering wanders about, so the letters move out of order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A promise that a winding path will certainly lead you to a rainbow.
annotation.walkthrough: 'For certain' looks like padding meaning 'definitely', but it supplies every letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A rainbow appears when sunlight is refracted, bent and split, by raindrops.

entries.clue: Carries out belongings (7)

blocks.note: to effect a plan is to carry it out
the plural noun for what a person owns, used in wills and police property bags

annotation.surface: Someone carries their belongings out of a house.
annotation.walkthrough: Read as a phrase, 'carries out belongings' is a removal; split in two, it is a verb and a noun that share one spelling.
annotation.definitionFit: Effects is both a verb meaning carries out and a noun meaning personal possessions.

entries.clue: Contemptible sort oversees conveniences for motorists (but not residents) (3,4)

blocks.note: a rat is a contemptible person
to run a business is to oversee it

annotation.surface: A despised official is in charge of roadside facilities for drivers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Conveniences' suggests public toilets; here it is shortcuts. A rat run is a side street drivers use to dodge main-road traffic, to the annoyance of people living there.
annotation.definitionFit: Rat runs are handy for drivers cutting through, and a nuisance to the residents of those streets.

entries.clue: What may be seen all around Lancashire? (11)

annotation.definition: What may be seen all around Lancashire?

blocks.clueFragment: What may be seen all around
blocks.note: surface reading: something visible everywhere; setter's reading: a wrapping that goes round the outside of something
surface reading: the English county; setter's reading: the crumbly cheese named after it

annotation.surface: A question about something visible everywhere in the county of Lancashire.
annotation.walkthrough: Lancashire reads as the English county; it is the crumbly cheese named after it, traditionally matured wrapped in cheesecloth.
annotation.definitionFit: Cheesecloth is the loose cotton gauze wrapped all around a cheese such as Lancashire.

entries.clue: Everyman had to take on assistant, one dealing with email etc (4)

indicatorNotes.to take on: to take on staff is to bring them in, so PA goes inside I'D

blocks.note: the setter, Everyman, refers to himself as I; I had = I'D
PA = personal assistant
the 'd of I'D, short for had

annotation.surface: The setter complains he had to hire an assistant to deal with his email.
annotation.walkthrough: A setter's name in a clue means I or ME; here 'Everyman had' is I'D, which takes PA inside.
annotation.definitionFit: An iPad is a tablet computer, a device you deal with email and the like on.

entries.clue: Nightingale's wings in site of literary murder (4)

indicatorNotes.wings: a bird's wings are at its sides, so take the letters at each edge of the word

blocks.note: the left-hand edge of NIGHTINGALE
the right-hand edge of NIGHTINGALE

annotation.surface: A nightingale's feathers turn up at the scene of a crime from a novel.
annotation.walkthrough: The wings here are two letters each, not one. The literary murder is Agatha Christie's Death on the Nile.
annotation.definitionFit: Agatha Christie's Death on the Nile sets its murder on a steamer on the river.

entries.clue: Organiser of libraries said to be somewhat wet (4)

indicatorNotes.said: what is said is spoken, so the answer sounds like the name

blocks.note: Melvil Dewey devised the Dewey Decimal system for shelving library books

annotation.surface: A librarian is described as a bit damp.
annotation.walkthrough: The organiser is Melvil Dewey, whose Dewey Decimal Classification numbers the shelves in libraries worldwide.
annotation.definitionFit: Dewy means covered in dew, lightly moist.

entries.clue: No longer enjoying Pink Floyd album? Crazy (3-3-4)

blocks.note: to go off something is to stop liking it
The Wall is Pink Floyd's 1979 album

annotation.surface: Someone who has gone off a Pink Floyd record calls it mad.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Crazy' sits after the question mark as a separate verdict, so the definition is at the end, not with the album.
annotation.definitionFit: Off-the-wall means bizarre or unconventional, near enough crazy.

entries.clue: Scarce enough to manage? Take a new approach (6,6)

indicatorNotes.to manage: to manage letters is to handle and arrange them into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: If supplies are only just sufficient to get by, a change of plan is needed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Scarce enough to manage' reads as a complaint about rations; every letter of 'scarce enough' is in the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom from sailing and flying: altering your heading, used figuratively for adopting a different plan.

entries.clue: Fidgety recluse agog, seeing Hollywood big-shot (6,5)

indicatorNotes.Fidgety: something fidgety cannot keep still, so the letters shift about

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A restless hermit is thrilled to meet a film mogul.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface has a hermit starstruck by a mogul; the mogul is made of the hermit's own letters.
annotation.definitionFit: George Lucas created Star Wars and is one of Hollywood's most powerful filmmakers.

entries.clue: Had fun? Noted (10)

blocks.note: to celebrate is to have a party
noted as an adjective: famous, well known

annotation.surface: A question and a curt reply: did you enjoy yourself? Point taken.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Noted' looks like a verb, 'I have written that down'; it is the adjective, famous.
annotation.definitionFit: Celebrated is the past tense of celebrate, making merry, and an adjective meaning famous.

entries.clue: Gentle swab for treatment somewhere in India (4,6)

indicatorNotes.for treatment: what is sent for treatment gets worked on, so the letters are reworked

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A doctor uses a soft swab to treat a patient somewhere in India.
annotation.walkthrough: The medical surface makes 'for treatment' look like part of the story; it tells you to rework 'gentle swab'.
annotation.definitionFit: West Bengal is a state in eastern India, capital Kolkata.

entries.clue: Footwear? They've got cloven hooves! (7)

blocks.note: Reebok is a brand of trainers
the reebok, or rhebok, is a small South African antelope

annotation.surface: Asked what is on their feet, someone jokes that they have hooves.
annotation.walkthrough: The trainer brand took its name from the antelope, so the two definitions are the same word.
annotation.definitionFit: A trade name for the first sense; for the second, the Afrikaans-derived name of a small grey South African antelope, also spelt rhebok.

entries.clue: Hide in quarter of Greek island? (7)

blocks.note: SE, south-east, is a quarter of the compass
Crete is the largest Greek island

annotation.surface: Someone goes into hiding in one district of a Greek island.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like it puts one thing inside another; here it only joins the definition to the wordplay, and 'quarter of' is a compass point placed before the island.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to conceal, from the same Latin root as secret.

entries.clue: Caretaker sent back copper and silver vessels (7)

indicatorNotes.sent back: what is sent back returns the way it came, so the letters run right to left

blocks.note: a copper is a penny coin, abbreviated P
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
pots are vessels

annotation.surface: A caretaker returns some copper and silver containers.
annotation.walkthrough: Copper here is the coin, not Cu. Caretaker means a temporary stand-in, as in a caretaker manager.
annotation.definitionFit: A caretaker manager or government is a stopgap, filling in until a permanent one arrives.

entries.clue: Guide is glib, high-flying type (7)

blocks.note: a pat answer is glib, too ready
a tern is a seabird

annotation.surface: A tour guide is dismissed as smooth-talking and ambitious.
annotation.walkthrough: 'High-flying type' suggests a go-getter; it is literally a bird.
annotation.definitionFit: A pattern is a model or template to guide you, as in dressmaking.

entries.clue: It might be some homework, Chuck (7)

blocks.note: a piece of schoolwork done over weeks, often at home
as a verb: to throw, hurl or cast forward

annotation.surface: A parent tells a child named Chuck that this could be homework.
annotation.walkthrough: Chuck looks like a boy's name being addressed; it is the verb, to throw.
annotation.definitionFit: Project is both a school assignment and a verb meaning to hurl.

entries.clue: A printmaker has these urges (7)

blocks.note: the machines a printmaker squeezes inked plates onto paper with
to press someone is to urge them

annotation.surface: An artist who makes prints is said to have strong impulses.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Urges' reads as a noun after 'has these'; it is the verb.
annotation.definitionFit: Presses are the machines a printmaker uses, and presses means urges.

entries.clue: Fashionista puts on bridle, saddle, etc? (7,5)

blocks.note: a person who loves dressing up and showing off the latest fashions
read the answer as a verb and its object: dresses the animal in its tack

annotation.surface: A fashion lover tries on horse tack.
annotation.walkthrough: The second half reads the answer as a verb and object: someone who clothes a horse puts on its bridle and saddle. The question mark flags the stretch.
annotation.definitionFit: A clothes horse is a person devoted to dressing fashionably.

entries.clue: Lamb and Teddy regularly tucked up (4)

indicatorNotes.regularly: regularly means at even intervals, so take every other letter

blocks.note: second and fourth letters of lAmB
second and fourth letters of tEdDy

annotation.surface: A child's toy lamb and teddy bear are tucked up in bed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'And' only joins the two words; the even letters are taken from Lamb and Teddy separately.
annotation.definitionFit: Abed means in bed, tucked up for the night.

entries.clue: Sport unleashing mammoth opponents, primarily? (4)

indicatorNotes.primarily: primarily means first of all, so take the first letter of each word before it

blocks.note: first letters of Sport, Unleashing, Mammoth, Opponents

annotation.surface: A sport that sets huge opponents loose on each other.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: sumo is the sport of enormous wrestlers.
annotation.definitionFit: Sumo is Japanese wrestling between very heavy opponents.

entries.clue: Conservative: I'm ready for my photo and something to eat (4,6)

blocks.note: blue is the colour of the UK Conservative party
'Cheese!' is what you say to smile for the camera

annotation.surface: A Tory politician poses for a photo and wants a snack.
annotation.walkthrough: In British politics the Conservatives are blue, so a Conservative is a Blue.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: blue-veined Stilton or Roquefort is one kind of food.

entries.clue: Male host, agreeable – to some extent (4)

indicatorNotes.to some extent: only part of the words is used, so the answer lies within them

blocks.note: hoSTAGreeable

annotation.surface: A man hosting a party is fairly pleasant.
annotation.walkthrough: The dash sets off the indicator; the answer runs across the comma from 'host' into 'agreeable'.
annotation.definitionFit: Stag means for men only, as in a stag party.

entries.clue: Lethargy resulting from some heated rows in Essex (10)

indicatorNotes.some: only some of the words is used, so the answer lies within them

blocks.note: heateDROWSINESSex

annotation.surface: Arguments in Essex leave everyone worn out.
annotation.walkthrough: Essex is an English county east of London; here it only supplies the letters ESS.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both name the heavy sluggishness of someone about to nod off.

entries.clue: Behold: Detective Inspector's flipping hero (4)

indicatorNotes.flipping: what is flipped is turned over, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: lo! is an old word for behold
DI is the abbreviation for Detective Inspector

annotation.surface: Look: the police inspector is a hero, and a bloody one at that.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' reads as a mild British swear word, as in 'flipping hero'; its job is to reverse LO DI.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a pop or sporting idol is looked up to as a hero.
